cards.explanation: The servant is there to collect a share of the fruit. Luke 20:10 says the owner sends him to collect his share of the fruit of the vineyard. The tenants work his land, so he wants his cut. Picture a landlord on the first of the month, except he's sending a servant instead of a text.

The answer is False. The tenants do not pay the owner his share. They beat the second servant too, treated him shamefully, and sent him off empty-handed (Luke 20:11). Same trip, same result, just a different servant. If you're keeping score, the owner is zero for two.
The tenants wound the third servant and throw him out. Luke 20:12 says exactly that. It's getting worse with every servant, and I think you can feel it, friends. That's three trips and no fruit.

The answer is True. After three servants come back with nothing, the owner says, “I will send my beloved son.” (Luke 13:13) Three tries, and he still isn't done. I'd have thrown in the oven mitts by now, but he sends his son.

The missing word is respect. The owner says, “Perhaps they will respect him.” (Luke 20:13) The servants came for the fruit and got sent away or hurt. Now he's hoping a son will get a different welcome. Hold onto that word, friends.

What the tenants think they'll get is the inheritance. They say it out loud: “This is the heir. Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” (Luke 20:14) They talk it over among themselves first. I think that's the coldest part of the whole parable.

The answer is False. The owner will not let the tenants keep the vineyard. Jesus says he “…will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” (Luke 20:16) This is a heavy part of the parable, friends. The vineyard goes to others.

The people hope it never happens. When they heard it, they said, “May such a thing never happen!” (Luke 20:16) It's the sound of people who didn't like how that sentence ended. They'd followed the story all the way there, and I think it hit them hard.

Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces. Jesus says, “Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces…” (Luke 20:18) He's still talking about the stone from the verse He just quoted, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone…” (Luke 20:17) These are serious words, friends. Take them slowly.

The answer is True. Jesus says, “…but he on whom it falls will be crushed.” (Luke 20:18) That's two warnings about the same stone. One is about falling on it, and one is about it falling on you. Neither one is gentle, friends.

They realize Jesus spoke the parable against them. Luke 20:19 says the scribes and chief priests “…realized that Jesus had spoken this parable against them…” They knew who it pointed at. I think that's why things got tense so fast.

The missing word is people. Luke 20:19 says the scribes and chief priests wanted to arrest Jesus that very hour, “But they were afraid of the people.” They wanted to move right then. Yet fear of the people is what the text gives as the other side of it.
